prize_parts.citation: for the invention and realisation of optical lattice clocks that brought frequency and time measurement to the 10^-18 level

statement.case_for: I keep B015 as a two-name prize. Katori's magic-wavelength lattice cancels the light shift while thousands of atoms are interrogated in parallel, and Ye's strontium work demonstrated the stability and systematic control that turned 10^-18 from a projection into a measured fact. The result has been reproduced and surpassed by independent laboratories using Sr, Yb and Hg, and it is already used for tests of relativity, searches for varying constants and dark matter, and relativistic geodesy. Round 1 supplied no named alternative or third name for the credit: nobody argued that a specific individual should replace or join Katori and Ye, so the two-name configuration stands. This is the only leading candidate where the credit follows the discovery without forcing an exclusion among the credited names.
statement.case_against: Distinctness from the 2005 comb and 2012 ion-control prizes remains the main reservation, and I accept that it is a judgement and not a settled point. Other lattice-clock groups (SYRTE, PTB, NIST and JILA colleagues, RIKEN) are not carried by the two names. Danielsson-Ulf, Johansson-Goran and Eriksson-Olle also make a fair point that B017 opened a new regime of physics while B015 delivers a new measurement capability. If the committee ranks breadth of new physics above precision, B017 should come first and I would not object. B015 also draws first-place support only from members who are themselves instrument-minded, which is a warning about my own bias.

responses.point: Danielsson holds that B015 is a deep refinement of precision built on the comb and ion-clock prizes, whereas moire graphene opened a new regime of physics, and says B015 would still be an honourable choice if clean attribution is valued most.
responses.response: I have thought about the criterion you put forward, new regime versus new capability, and I do not think it should override the evidence here. The prize criterion is a discovery or invention of greatest benefit, and the lattice clock is a distinct invention, not just a refinement: the comb counts optical cycles, the 2012 prize concerned control of single quantum systems, and neither gives the magic-wavelength many-atom architecture that reached 10^-18. I do accept that B017 is broader in reach, and that is why it is my first alternative. My preference stays with B015 because the credit and the reproduction are cleaner, but if the committee decides breadth of new physics is decisive, I would not block B017.

responses.point: Eriksson prefers B051 because topological insulators already changed what condensed-matter researchers compute and measure, while the clock's payoff for basic physics, redefinition of the second and dark-matter searches, is still prospective.
responses.response: I agree that the redefinition of the second is a policy step still to come, but I do not think the payoff is only prospective. Clock comparisons already constrain variation of constants and dark-matter couplings and have demonstrated gravitational redshift across millimetres, which are measurements with consequences for fundamental physics now. I also note that your own case against B051, thin support, contested third seat between Mele and Hasan, and Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang outside the names, is the credit problem that B015 does not have. I respect that B051 is the most mature discovery in the group, but I cannot rank it above B015 under the credit and support evidence in front of us.

responses.point: Mehlig moved to B017 after finding no support for B003, and argues that five top-three rankings from different subfields is better evidence of breadth than one enthusiast; Mehlig also notes that Bistritzer may pad the theory side.
responses.response: Your reasoning for moving from B003 to B017 is the correct kind of update, and I note it, but top-three counts are only one of several things I weigh. On the Bistritzer point, I think you identify the real weakness in the three-name B017: if the committee takes two names, MacDonald and Jarillo-Herrero, Yuan Cao is still outside, and the same critique that I make of B015 for other clock groups applies with more force there, because the discovery paper was a team effort. I would regard B017 with two names as defensible, but not cleaner than B015.

responses.point: Pearce, the chair, prefers B015 and regards the redefinition of the second as an open question about whether the committee should wait, and records competing lattice-clock groups at SYRTE, PTB and NIST as not carried by the two names.
responses.response: I agree on B015 and on the competing groups. On waiting, I now lean the other way from where I stood in round 1: the redefinition is a decision by metrology bodies based on the performance that Katori's and Ye's clocks already delivered, so the invention and its demonstration are complete regardless of when the second changes. Waiting would only make sense if the scientific claim were uncertain, and it is not. We should also guard against two instrument-minded members agreeing for shared reasons, which I said in round 1 and still hold.

responses.point: Johansson places B017 first, finds the credit split of B015 clean, and says the clock refines a quantity that is already well measured while moire systems opened an entirely new set of phenomena; Johansson is less relaxed about the maturity of a 2018 discovery.
responses.response: I accept your framing, and your own remark on maturity helps me: a 2018 discovery with an unresolved mechanism is a legitimate reason for patience that you applied to your own candidate. I would only say that 'already measured very well' understates the change, because a factor of about 100 in systematic uncertainty beyond the caesium standard is what enables the new tests. I would support B017 if a compact citation limited to the flat-band prediction and the observation of the correlated states is agreed, but I would not put it ahead of B015 this year.

uncertainties: Whether the committee reads the lattice clock as distinct from the 2005 and 2012 prizes or as an increment; my view rests on the magic-wavelength many-atom architecture, which I consider separate, but I may be biased as an atomic physicist.
Priority among early lattice-clock experiments and whether other groups deserve a place; I have not verified this independently and no member named a replacement for Katori or Ye.
Whether breadth of new physics (B017) should outweigh credit cleanliness and reproduction (B015), which is a committee value judgement and not a fact I can settle.
Whether the Yuan Cao and other experimental credit problems in B017 can be resolved by citation wording.
statement.conflict_note: No direct tie to Katori or Ye is documented in my profile. Adjacent connections for the recusal question raised by the chair: a doctoral-period research stay in John Hall's laboratory in Boulder, where combs and precision spectroscopy lineage is part of the background of B015, although Hall is not a candidate; and shared laser-stabilisation techniques with clock work. My quantum-memory and quantum-information work, WACQT involvement and Deep Light Vision are close to B016, B011, B010, B012 and B029, so I discount my views on those. I do not believe any recusal is required for B015, and I leave that to the committee.
